title: Sum the surprises, fading as you go
allegory: GAE credits each move with the commentator's surprises that follow it: after every step she says how much better things went than she expected, and a move's credit is the sum of the upcoming surprises, each counted a little less the further away it is.
map: the commentator's expectation at each moment
a surprise: things went this much better than expected
the TD residual δₜ = rₜ + γV(sₜ₊₁) − V(sₜ)
crediting a move with the surprises ahead, each counted less
λ: 0 is one-step (calm, biased), 1 is Monte Carlo (honest, noisy)
the final whistle resets the count
the termination mask (1 − dₜ₊₁): no credit crosses an episode boundary

cap.1: You sacrifice a piece and win forty moves later. Was it good? The next position says blunder; the final result says brilliant, but not which move earned it.
cap.2: The policy loss needs an advantage per action: did it beat expectations? Trusting the critic's next-step guess is stable but biased; waiting for the whole return is honest but noisy.
cap.3: A(sₜ, aₜ) must be built from rewards plus V. One-step TD is low-variance but inherits V's bias; the Monte Carlo return is unbiased but carries every later reward's noise.

cap.1: After each step, a commentator says how much better things went than she expected. Credit a move with the next few surprises, each later one counting less.
cap.2: Each TD residual δ is a surprise: reward plus the critic's new estimate, minus its old one. GAE credits an action with the surprises ahead, weighted by (γλ)¹, (γλ)² and so on.
cap.3: GAE(λ) is the exponentially weighted average of every n-step advantage estimator, which telescopes to Σₗ (γλ)ˡ δₜ₊ₗ: a geometric sum of TD residuals (Schulman et al., 2016).

cap.1: Add up the surprises ahead, shrinking each by the same factor per step. That factor, γ times λ, sets how far ahead you listen.
cap.2: In code it is one reverse pass: A[t] = δ[t] + (1 − d[t+1])·γ·λ·A[t+1], starting from A[T−1] = δ[T−1]. The critic's regression target becomes A + V.
cap.3: Effective horizon ≈ 1/(1 − γλ): about 17 steps at γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95. The same mask belongs inside δ, since there is no V(sₜ₊₁) to bootstrap from across a termination.

cap.1: Turn λ up and you listen further ahead; turn it down and you mostly trust the commentator. At λ = 0.95 a surprise 17 steps away still counts about a third.
cap.2: Weights on future surprises: λ = 0 keeps only δₜ (one-step TD), λ = 1 keeps all of them (Monte Carlo), and 0.95 is the usual middle. γ and λ multiply.
cap.3: Weights (γλ)ˡ at γ = 0.99. λ trades bias from V's errors (λ → 0) against variance from reward noise (λ → 1); horizon 1/(1 − γλ) ≈ 17 at λ = 0.95.

chapters.name: The leaky boundary

left.title: mask applied
lines: credit stops at the final whistle
last step's A equals its δ

right.title: mask missing
lines: λ < 1 hides it as it fades
λ = 1 runs it the whole way

chapters.verdict: Test it: an episode's last advantage must equal its own δ.

cap.1: When a game ends, the count must stop. Forget, and surprises from the next game leak back into this one. A little fading hides the bug; no fading exposes it.
cap.2: Without the (1 − d) mask, advantages leak across episode boundaries, and λ < 1 hides it because the leak decays. Unit test: two episodes; the last step's A must equal its δ.
cap.3: Mask both the recursion and δ's bootstrap. At λ = 1 the critic no longer reduces variance, so runs turn seed-dependent, and an unmasked leak spans the whole rollout.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: λ is the dial when credit looks wrong
Same fading sum as eligibility traces

cap.1: PPO, which RLHF uses to train language models, feeds on these advantages. If credit is wrong here, everything downstream learns the wrong lesson.
cap.2: A wrong GAE looks like a broken PPO. When credit assignment looks off, check the mask, then tune λ. GAE also upgrades the critic's own target to a lookahead.
cap.3: In PPO-based RLHF, per-token advantages decide which tokens get reinforced; GAE is a common way to compute them, so it shapes how reward and KL signals steer a model.

caption.1: Each bar is a step's credit. At λ = 0 only t3 gets credit for the win; slide λ up and credit spreads back. Then switch the mask off: episode 2 leaks into t3.
caption.2: Toy critic: V = 0.2 in episode 1, 0.5 in episode 2. With the mask on, A at t3 always equals its own δ, 0.8. With it off, episode 2's failure drags t3 down, or its V leaks into the bootstrap.
caption.3: A computed by the reverse pass with mask (1 − m·dₜ₊₁) in both δ and the recursion. Unmasked, λ = 0.95 gives A₃ ≈ 0.39 instead of 0.80: exactly the boundary-leak unit test.

Exponential moving averages anywhere: recent evidence counts most, older evidence fades
PPO-based RLHF: per-token advantages decide which tokens a language model is pushed toward

hamming.what: A way to score each action by adding up the critic's surprises that follow it, each counted less the further away, with λ setting how fast the counting fades.
hamming.when: Every time you train PPO or another actor-critic method; you write compute_advantages in [2.3].
hamming.why: It lets you choose a point between a calm but biased estimate and an honest but noisy one, which is what made policy gradients stable enough for hard control problems.

object.title: The fading staircase
object.subtitle: Rows are λ settings, columns are steps ahead; each bar is how much a future surprise still counts.

cap.1: Each row is a λ setting; each column is a few steps further ahead. A bar's height is how much that future surprise still counts.
cap.2: Weights (γλ)ˡ for l = 0, 3, 6 ... 33, one row per λ, at γ = 0.99.
cap.3: Row r plots (γλᵣ)ˡ: the kernel GAE convolves with the TD residuals.

cap.1: λ = 0 keeps only the very next surprise: one bar. λ = 1 keeps them all, fading only because of γ.
cap.2: λ = 0 is one-step TD; λ = 1 is Monte Carlo minus V. Everything else sits between.
cap.3: Endpoints: λ = 0 gives δₜ (bias from V); λ = 1 telescopes to the return minus V (variance from rewards).

cap.1: The usual λ = 0.95 row still counts about a third at 17 steps ahead, then fades out.
cap.2: At γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95 the weight is about 0.35 at 17 steps: the effective horizon.

cap.1: Lower γ and every row fades faster. The two dials multiply, so both shorten how far ahead you listen.
cap.2: γ and λ compound: cutting γ to 0.9 shrinks every row's reach, even at λ = 1.
cap.3: The kernel depends only on the product γλ; γ also changes the objective, whereas λ changes only the estimator.
